title: Dynamic Programming Basics

steps.title: Recognize repeated subproblems
steps.content: Dynamic programming (DP) solves a problem by reusing results of smaller subproblems instead of recalculating them. It is useful when subproblems overlap and an optimal solution can be built from optimal smaller solutions.
steps.example: Naive recursive Fibonacci recalculates fib(2) many times.

steps.title: Choose a DP signal
steps.prompt: Which property suggests that dynamic programming may help?
steps.explanation: DP saves work when the same smaller subproblems are solved repeatedly.

steps.title: Memoization versus tabulation
steps.content: Memoization is top-down: solve recursively and store each result. Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table from base cases toward the answer.
steps.example: For Fibonacci, store fib(0), fib(1), then compute each next value once.

steps.title: Find Fibonacci
steps.prompt: Using fib(0)=0 and fib(1)=1, what is fib(5)?

steps.title: Define the state and transition
steps.content: A DP solution needs a state (what a subproblem represents), a transition (how states depend on smaller states), base cases and an evaluation order.
steps.tip: Before writing code, write the meaning of dp[i] in one sentence.

questions.explanation: Memoization stores previously computed results for reuse.
Tabulation computes smaller states first and fills the table toward the final state.

questions.prompt: Which two properties commonly support DP?
questions.explanation: DP benefits from repeated subproblems and solutions built from smaller optimal solutions.

questions.prompt: With fib(0)=0 and fib(1)=1, what is fib(6)?
What should a DP state clearly define?
options: What each stored subproblem value means
questions.explanation: A precise state definition makes the recurrence and base cases understandable.

learning_objectives: Recognize overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.
Define a state and recurrence before coding.
Set base cases and verify transition dependencies.

common_misconceptions.correction: DP stores results of overlapping subproblems to avoid recomputation.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A recurrence alone is a complete solution.
common_misconceptions.correction: You also need correct base cases, evaluation order and state boundaries.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Memoization and tabulation are identical implementations.
common_misconceptions.correction: Memoization is top-down; tabulation fills states bottom-up.

worked_examples.title: Fibonacci with memoization
trace: Later requests reuse stored values instead of recalculating.
worked_examples.explanation: Caching removes the repeated exponential recursion tree.

worked_examples.title: Climbing stairs
worked_examples.input: 1 or 2 steps at a time; reach step n
worked_examples.explanation: The final step comes from either n-1 or n-2.

worked_examples.title: Choose DP state
worked_examples.input: Minimum coins to make amount x
trace: State dp[x] = fewest coins for amount x.
Base dp[0]=0; other amounts start unreachable.
Try each coin c: dp[x]=min(dp[x],1+dp[x-c]) when valid.
worked_examples.explanation: A precise state definition makes the transition and boundaries easier to verify.

company_applications.practice: Explain state, transition and base case before code.
Start with small n and trace the table.
Analyze time and memory in terms of states and transitions.

srs_cards.question: What should you remember about Dynamic Programming Basics?
srs_cards.answer: Recognize overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Define a state and recurrence before coding. Choose memoization or tabulation. Set base cases and verify transition dependencies.

srs_cards.question: What mistake should you avoid in Dynamic Programming Basics?
srs_cards.answer: DP stores results of overlapping subproblems to avoid recomputation.
